dailyRead: This is a Sunday page, so there is no new tape to read - TE's currency and commodity boards still print Friday's Sep/18 closes, EUR/USD 1.14851, USD/JPY 156.874, DXY 100.222, WTI 100.300, gold 4383.45 - and the useful work is therefore entirely in the two things that have changed underneath those unchanged prices. The first is a reversal this page owes an explanation for. Since the RBNZ hiked to 2.75% on September 2, every New Zealand note here has rested on a single asymmetry, stated most sharply yesterday: New Zealand has the largest energy-driven inflation overshoot on the board at 4.1%, and a central bank that has said it will look through it, with TE carrying no further hike - the exact mirror of a Bank of England with 3.1% inflation and three members voting to tighten. That asymmetry is what put NZD last at -1, what made NZD/USD the widest score gap available at four points and the highest-conviction dollar ticket on the page, and what justified AUD/NZD and GBP/NZD longs. It is no longer what the canonical source says. TE's interest-rate calendar for New Zealand now carries a TEForecast of 3.0% at the December 9 meeting, and TE's model text projects the official cash rate trending around 4.00% in 2027 and 3.75% in 2028. Read those two rows together and New Zealand has the steepest projected tightening path of any currency on this board: +125bp from today's 2.75%, against the Fed's own projected move from 4.00% to 4.25%, against an RBA that TE has EASING to 4.10% next year, and against a euro area TE holds at 2.65% before cutting to 2.15% in 2028. The corroboration outside TE is consistent and it sharpens the point rather than softening it: Governor Anna Breman said following the September 2 decision that a further rate increase is likely and that the Bank simply wants time to assess how the hikes delivered so far are flowing through, Assistant Governor Karen Silk's remarks moved investors to price the next move for December rather than October, and the RBNZ now expects headline inflation will not return to the 2% midpoint until early 2028 - later than previously projected, which is a hawkish revision. The honest reading is that this page mistook a pause for an absence. A central bank that has hiked twice in three months, whose governor says more is likely, whose own forecast pushes target convergence out by a year, and whose canonical path carries a December hike is not looking through 4.1% inflation; it is spacing its response. So NZD goes from -1 to 0, and the specific fact that changed is TE's December 9 row. What does not change is the domestic weakness that keeps it from going higher, and it is genuinely bad: unemployment 5.6% and rising from 5.4%, Q2 GDP slowing to +0.2% q/q from +0.9%, wage growth just 2.1%, retail sales -0.5% m/m, business confidence down to 53.7 from 56.1, and a currency that is still the worst performer on the board at -1.58% on the week and -3.62% on the month. October 28 is a hold on TE's own forecast. So this is 0 and not +1, and the trades move accordingly rather than flipping: NZD/USD stays SHORT on a three-point gap but drops to LOW-MED and is no longer the page's best dollar expression, AUD/NZD stays LONG at LOW-MED on a two-point gap instead of three, GBP/NZD falls to a one-point gap, EUR/NZD goes RANGE, and NZD/JPY turns LONG because the kiwi now outranks the yen. The second change is the one that no price on this page has seen yet, and it is the reason a Sunday page matters this week. Germany votes today in Berlin and in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. These are the two state elections that follow the September 6 Saxony-Anhalt vote where the AfD came close to an outright majority, and the reporting into the weekend is unambiguous about the stakes: Merz's CDU is expected to lose ground in both, and heavy losses across the pair would leave the Chancellor under immediate pressure to step aside well before the 2029 federal election. Markets closed on Friday afternoon, hours before polls, so whatever comes out tonight reaches the euro and the DAX cold at Monday's open, and Lagarde then speaks twice into the aftermath, Monday at 15:00Z and Tuesday at 11:00Z. The disciplined response is to hold EUR at 0 rather than to pre-position. That is not caution for its own sake - it is the lesson of this page's own mistake on Friday, when it cut JPY only after Ueda's press conference had actually happened rather than in anticipation of it, and was right to wait. A binary political event is not a score input until it resolves. What it IS is a reason to change how the euro leg is held: EUR/GBP short stays the featured trade because it is a reaction-function trade that survives either result, EUR/USD stays SHORT on the three-point rate gap, and GER40 goes from directional to RANGE because a German equity index carrying an unresolved German political result into a Monday gap is a levels trade, not a direction trade. The dollar needs a correction rather than an update, and it runs the other way from what a correction usually means. Yesterday's page asserted twice that TE's calendar carries a 4% forecast at the October 28 FOMC and used that to dismiss weekend commentary about October hike pricing. Re-reading the row directly, that is wrong: the October 28 line shows Previous 4% with the Actual, Consensus and TEForecast cells all empty. TE publishes no meeting-level forecast for October. What TE does publish is a model path - 4.00% by the end of this quarter, then trending around 4.25 percent in 2027 and 4.00 percent in 2028 - which means the canonical source carries one further hike and simply does not date it. That is more hawkish than yesterday's framing, not less, and it removes the awkwardness of this page arguing against market pricing that runs around 56% for an October move. USD holds +3 on unchanged TE data: CPI 3.4% with core easing to 2.4%, unemployment 4.1%, non-farm payrolls +162K, retail control group +1.4%, services PMI 56.5, GDP annual 2.1%, initial claims 196K against a 206K previous with the four-week average 203,000. The two qualifiers stand - consumer confidence 47.8 from 51.7, and Warsh's line about not envisaging an aggressive cycle - and the week's inputs are thin by design: Goolsbee Monday, Williams and Jefferson Tuesday, flash PMIs Wednesday, claims Thursday with a 201K forecast, and revised UoM sentiment Friday at 47.5. August core PCE at month-end is still the real test of the 3.4% projection against core CPI already at 2.4%. Australia holds +2 and the canonical-versus-market split that this page flagged on Friday has widened rather than closed. Market pricing for a September 29 hike to 4.60% has firmed from the 70-75% quoted yesterday to a range of 80-87% depending on the source, and the sell-side has moved with it: NAB, Deutsche Bank, UBS and Morgan Stanley now forecast the hike at that meeting, ANZ and CBA carry November, and Westpac is alone in seeing no further increase this year. TE, the canonical source, still carries 4.35% unchanged at September 29 - and its model then projects Australia trending around 4.10% in 2027, which is easing. So the position is a currency priced at better than four-in-five odds for a hawkish outcome its canonical forecaster does not carry at all, and whose canonical medium-term path is lower. That is asymmetric against AUD, which is why the Australian longs continue to run against the weakest legs - AUD/JPY, AUD/CAD, AUD/CHF - and why AUD/USD stays RANGE despite the differential about to move Australia's way. One number to correct from yesterday: the consensus for Thursday's 01:30Z August labour force survey is +20.9K, not the roughly +15K this page carried, against July's -15,827, with the unemployment rate forecast unchanged at 4.5%. A second consecutive contraction against a raised consensus, three business days before the board meets, is what takes AUD to +1. Sterling holds +1 and the case picked up quiet corroboration from TE's own model. Britain's projected path is 4.00 percent in 2027 against today's 3.75%, so the canonical source carries the hike that three of nine MPC members were already voting for on September 17 - TE still shows those vote rows explicitly, Vote Hike 3/9 and Vote Cut 0/9 - and the November 5 decision carries no TE forecast either way. A smaller detail worth noting rather than leaning on: TE's calendar lists December 17 with a BoE MPC Vote Unchanged row and a Vote Hike row scheduled, and no Vote Cut row. The energy case behind Friday's upgrade is unchanged - Ofgem's confirmed October 1 cap rise of 4% to 1,723 pounds with the gas component up 8%, blamed on the Middle East conflict, a further 9% pencilled in for Q1 2027, UK gas at 198.16 and +26.71% on the month - and so is the offset that caps it: the same announcement zeroes VAT on domestic electricity from October 1 to March 31, mechanically flattering the October CPI the MPC sees on November 5. The labour market remains the restraint, with the claimant count +27.8K against an 8.3K forecast, payrolled employees -26.1K and wage growth decelerating to 3.9%. This week gives four separate reads on that committee: Dhingra, Breeden and Lombardelli all speak Thursday, and Bailey Friday at 09:15Z. EUR/GBP short is still the cleanest trade on the page, and the reason is now visible in the projections rather than only in the rhetoric: TE has Britain at 4.00% in 2027 and the euro area at 2.65% before cutting to 2.15%. Both economies are taking the identical gas shock - EU gas 79.52 and +25.46% on the month, German gas 80.54 and +25.91%, UK gas +26.71% - and only one central bank is expected to answer it. The euro area's final August HICP was revised down to 3.2% with services at 3.0% from 3.3% and core 2.4%, so what holds the headline up is energy at +14.3% y/y, precisely what the ECB looks through, and nothing is scheduled before the October 8 accounts. The cross at 0.85741 does not price that divergence, and it does not need the dollar to be right. The yen stays at -1 and the specific thing to know about it this week is the calendar, not the macro: Japan is closed Monday and Tuesday for back-to-back bank holidays, which thins the yen tape into an environment where intervention risk is already elevated. The structural case is unchanged - the BoJ hiked to 1.25% on September 18 in a 7-2 vote with Asada and Sato dissenting against, Ueda gave no explicit pace guidance, TE's October 30 row carries no forecast with Previous at 1.25%, and TE's model projects Japan trending around 1.00 percent in 2027, which is BELOW the current rate. Core CPI is 1.7%, under the 1.8% consensus and down from 1.8%. Against that, two restraints keep every yen cross at LOW-MED or MEDIUM rather than higher, and both are technical rather than fundamental: USD/JPY completed an evening star reversal on Thursday from the multi-decade high at 162.84, the first time in months the technical picture has not been one-way, and the Ministry of Finance bought yen twelve days ago at a better level than 156.87. The counterweight to the intervention fear is that the historic US-Japan operation earlier this year failed to halt the slide and mostly slowed it - so treat intervention as a sizing problem, not a direction problem. September 30's Summary of Opinions is the next scheduled input. Oil and the metals remain one trade, and the two-sidedness that kept USOIL at RANGE has if anything become better documented. Crude fell a third session to 100.300, -1.58%, finishing the week flat at +0.25% with Brent 103.870, because the market has been weighting Saudi Arabia's workarounds above the fighting. But Rapidan Energy's read is that the East-West pipeline outage constrains Saudi crude production and exports through at least the end of September, with risk skewed toward a larger disruption if it runs past September or if Iran, the Houthis or other proxies escalate - which is a firmer supply constraint than the half-capacity-back-within-days framing this page carried on Friday. And the chokepoint has not reopened: twelve vessels transited Hormuz on September 16 against six the day before, eleven of the twelve running dark with AIS switched off, against a pre-crisis baseline of 88 to 130 transits a day. Iran has been enforcing new maritime transit rules since its 60-day ceasefire lapsed, with a fatal attack on the bulk carrier Minoan Dignity and the seizure of the tanker Amara, while Foreign Minister Araghchi has claimed in Beijing that Iran has agreed a plan with Oman to reopen the strait - a claim no Omani official has confirmed. So crude is cheaper on logistics while the physical risk is unchanged or worse, which is an unstable equilibrium and the reason USOIL is RANGE with upward asymmetry and CAD stays at 0 rather than being cut. The metals keep taking the real-rate side of that: gold 4383.45 and +0.76% on the week though still -2.97% on the month, silver 66.236 and +3.07% on the week and the best thing on the commodity board, with the Silver Institute now putting 2026's deficit at 46.3 million ounces, a sixth consecutive shortfall and wider than last year's. Copper at 6.6150 and +2.25% on the week is the strongest structural story and the physical corroboration of the Australian view, with available LME stocks drained to roughly 90,000 tonnes and cash more than 550 dollars over three-month futures after the 14,533 record on September 7 - and worth noting, it is trading far above the 10,000-11,000 dollar range Goldman carries for 2026, which is a crowding warning as much as a bullish one. Canada stays at 0 with no rate support and no terms-of-trade help: TE carries 2.25% through October 28 and projects 2.25% in 2027, August CPI was -0.1% m/m leaving 3.0% annual, employment is -41,700 and services PMI 46.8. Macklem speaks Monday at 15:05Z and retail sales land Thursday with a -0.8% forecast. The franc stays at 0 into the only scheduled decision this board is directly exposed to. TE, the FF consensus and the economist polls all carry 0.00% for Thursday 07:30Z, so the rate is not the event - Schlegel's conditional inflation forecast and his language on FX intervention are, with the June assessment having signalled greater readiness to counter rapid franc appreciation. Swiss data runs hot for a zero policy rate: GDP 2.3% y/y, manufacturing PMI 57.1, CPI accelerating to 0.8% from 0.4%, harmonised 0.9%, unemployment 3.0%, with wage growth decelerating to 0.4% the main disinflationary line. USD/CHF at 0.82220 is +3.11% on the month, a franc weaker through a shooting war, which is what an intervention-ready central bank produces. One sourcing note: a commentary piece surfaced this weekend describing the SNB policy rate as 1.00% and Swiss CPI as -0.2% with USD/CHF near 0.89. None of that matches TE and none of it is used here. The cleanest four things on this page: EUR/GBP short on the reaction-function split, USD/JPY and AUD/JPY long on the widest gaps with sizing discipline, USD/CAD long, and silver. Nothing is HIGH conviction into a Monday open carrying an unpriced German election result, with the SNB and Australian jobs on Thursday and the RBA nine days out.

Core CPI 1.7%, under the 1.8% consensus and down from 1.8%; headline 1.9%; unemployment 2.4%; wage growth 4.7%; manufacturing PMI 54.9. strength.forward: 🔻 Now the sole occupant of the bottom after the kiwi's upgrade, and the canonical path is the cleanest part of the case: TE has Japan trending to 1.00% in 2027 against a Fed at 4.25%. The week's specific feature is the calendar - Japan is closed Monday and Tuesday, and a thinned tape is where intervention bites hardest. Two technical restraints keep the crosses at LOW-MED to MEDIUM: an evening star completed Thursday from the 162.84 multi-decade high, and the MoF buying yen twelve days ago at a better level. The offset is that the historic US-Japan operation mostly slowed the slide rather than halting it. Back to 0 on intervention or a hawkish Sep 30 Summary of Opinions.

symbols.why: Still the featured trade, and the split is now in TE's projections rather than only the rhetoric: TE has Britain trending around 4.00% in 2027 against today's 3.75%, and the euro area at 2.65% before cutting to 2.15% in 2028. Both economies take the identical gas shock - UK gas +26.71% on the month, EU gas +25.46% - and only one committee is expected to answer it, with three of nine already voting for 4% against an ECB whose services inflation fell to 3.0%.
symbols.risk: Tonight's German vote cuts both ways here: a benign result removes a euro headwind this ticket has not been paid for anyway. The VAT cut to zero on UK electricity from Oct 1 flatters October CPI down and gives the MPC cover to look through the cap too, and Bailey on Friday 09:15Z could say exactly that. Cross has been range-bound near 0.857 for weeks - it needs November pricing to build.

symbols.why: The widest score gap on the board at four points now that the kiwi has moved up, and the canonical paths diverge outright: TE projects the Fed trending around 4.25% in 2027 while projecting Japan at 1.00%, BELOW its current 1.25%. Ueda gave no pace guidance after a 7-2 hike with two dissents against, core CPI printed 1.7% under consensus, and the yen closed an eighth straight session weaker at 156.874 after trading past 157.
symbols.risk: Size this one down rather than up. Thursday completed an evening star from the 162.84 multi-decade high - the first time in months the technical picture has not been one-way - and the MoF bought yen twelve days ago at a better level. Japan being shut Monday and Tuesday thins the tape, which is where intervention bites hardest and where a gap against you is most likely. USD/JPY is still -0.82% on the MONTH.

symbols.why: Three-point gap and the cleanest way to hold the Australian view without the dollar in the ticket: markets price 80-87% for an RBA hike to 4.60% on Sep 29 with four major banks now forecasting it, against a BoJ whose canonical path runs BELOW its current rate. At 111.72 with the yen down an eighth session and copper +2.25% on the week backing the Australian leg.
symbols.risk: Two-sided event risk in one position - Thursday's 01:30Z Australian jobs against a raised +20.9K consensus, and intervention that happened twelve days ago at a better level than 156.87. TE carries no RBA hike at all and projects easing to 4.10% next year, so the Australian leg is a market view. A risk-off shock hits this pair harder than anything else on the page.

symbols.why: Best performer on the commodity board at 66.236, +1.60% on the day and +3.07% on the week, with the real-rate mechanism working plainly: crude falling three sessions pulls inflation expectations and real yields down. The industrial leg adds what gold lacks, and the Silver Institute now puts 2026's deficit at 46.3 million ounces - a sixth consecutive shortfall and wider than last year's.
symbols.risk: Still -1.03% on the MONTH, so this is a recovery rather than a trend, and it fights a dollar at +3 whose canonical path carries another hike. If Rapidan is right that the Saudi outage constrains exports past end-September, crude turns back up and the inflation-expectations channel driving this reverses. Silver's industrial leg cuts both ways on any China disappointment.

The Canadian domestic side is the weakest on the board: employment -41,700, services PMI 46.8, retail sales -0.8% m/m and participation down to 65.0%. Week +0.82%, month +1.29%.
symbols.risk: This is short crude by proxy, and the crude read firmed against it this weekend - Rapidan sees the East-West pipeline constraining Saudi production and exports through at least end-September with risk skewed to a larger disruption. Hormuz at roughly 6-12 transits a day against an 88-130 baseline means the premium can return fast. Macklem speaks Monday 15:05Z. At 1.3986 the pair is near the top of its range and 1.40 is an obvious line.

symbols.why: Two-point gap between a disinflating euro area whose services inflation fell to 3.0% and core to 2.4%, with nothing scheduled before the Oct 8 accounts, and an Australia where 80-87% odds of a Sep 29 hike are priced and four major banks now forecast it. Rising gas makes the euro's terms of trade worse without buying a policy response, and the euro leg carries tonight's German result cold into Monday.
symbols.risk: Thursday's Australian jobs print against a +20.9K consensus is the shared risk with every AUD long here, and TE carries neither the hike nor the path. A German result tonight that is read as stabilising, plus an Oct 8 accounts revealing a Council worried about energy pass-through, firms the euro leg. Copper rolling over removes the corroborating signal.

symbols.why: The strongest structural story on the commodity board and the physical corroboration of the Australian view: 6.6150, +2.25% on the week and +1.97% on the month, after an LME record 14,533 dollars a tonne on Sep 7, available LME stocks drained to roughly 90,000 tonnes and cash trading more than 550 dollars over three-month futures, a backwardation last seen in 2021.
symbols.risk: Worth stating plainly as a crowding warning: at these levels copper trades far above the 10,000-11,000 dollar range Goldman carries for 2026. The squeeze is tariff-arbitrage driven - over a million tonnes pulled into US warehouses since early 2025 - so a tariff resolution or exemption change could release metal and unwind the backwardation fast. Chinese demand disappointment is the standing fundamental risk.

August core PCE at month-end confirming the 2.4% core deceleration rather than the 3.4% projection is the real threat.

Core PCE printing hot at month-end breaks the real-rate leg. Silver remains the better-supported of the two metals here.

Friday's -0.29% already shows the franc firming into the meeting, and weekly sight deposits are the tell to watch.

At 0.99603 the pair is pressed against parity, which has repeatedly capped it. Thursday brings both Australian jobs at 01:30Z and Canadian retail sales at 12:30Z.

Oct 28 is a hold on TE's forecast, so the December pricing has time to build against this position. Q3 CPI showing the fuel spike leaking into core would force the issue.

The UK labour market is the differentiator - claimant count +27.8K against an 8.3K forecast, payrolled employees -26.1K, wage growth decelerating to 3.9%.

At 1.33951 it was Friday's strongest major at +0.27%, and four committee reads land this week - Dhingra, Breeden and Lombardelli Thursday, Bailey Friday. A hawkish Bailey plus soft US claims reverses this quickly.

A hawkish Sep 30 Summary of Opinions reverses it.

Thursday's 01:30Z Australian labour force survey against a raised +20.9K consensus is the direct threat, and a soft print three business days before the board meets unwinds the pricing this depends on.

Down three sessions to 100.300, -1.58%, with the week flat at +0.25% because Saudi workarounds were weighted above the fighting - but Rapidan Energy now reads the damaged East-West pipeline as constraining Saudi crude production and exports through at least the end of September, with risk skewed toward a larger disruption.

The standing headwinds are unchanged: German gas +4.25% on the day and +25.91% on the month, and a tariff regime German exporters still cannot plan around. The tailwind is falling Brent at 103.870. Wait for the gap to resolve, then trade the level rather than the headline.

A soft Australian print plus a hawkish Bailey flips this outright. TE carries no RBA hike and projects Australia easing to 4.10% next year. At 1.88096 the pair has chopped without trend for a fortnight.

The two paths have converged.

The UK labour market has cracked and Bailey speaks Friday. NZD remains crowded short after -3.62% on the month, so this squeezes on any risk-on turn or a firm Q3 New Zealand CPI.

Three of nine MPC members are already voting to hike into a confirmed Oct 1 energy cap rise, against a Bank of Canada frozen by a -0.1% m/m CPI print with employment at -41,700.

The crude leg is the live threat: Rapidan reads the Saudi outage as constraining exports past end-September, and crude back above 110 pays Canada directly. Canadian retail sales Thursday 12:30Z at -0.8% forecast, Bailey Friday.

At 0.71214 the pair is -0.64% on the week and -0.05% on the month, which is the flattest thing on the board - the range is the honest read. A hike plus hawkish guidance on Sep 29 is what breaks it upward.

Japan is shut Monday and Tuesday, thinning one leg. An explicit SNB intervention threat plus a yen bid is the double loss here.

Canadian retail sales Thursday at -0.8% forecast and Macklem Monday 15:05Z are the near catalysts.

That is a +300bp projected spread by 2027.

New Zealand's domestic data is genuinely poor - unemployment 5.6% and rising, Q2 GDP +0.2% q/q, wage growth 2.1% - and the kiwi is still the board's worst performer at -3.62% on the month. On the yen side, intervention and the 162.84 evening star cap it, and Japan is shut Monday and Tuesday.

The euro leg is neutral rather than supportive, with services inflation down to 3.0% and core 2.4%.

That is a reason to wait for the gap rather than to carry through it. Lagarde speaks Monday 15:00Z and Tuesday 11:00Z.

Static scores, divergent paths.

New Zealand's labour market is deteriorating with unemployment 5.6% and rising, which is the argument for the euro leg if the vote passes benignly.

The euro area is disinflating with services at 3.0% and core 2.4%; Switzerland has CPI at 0.8% and a policy rate every source expects to stay at 0.00% on Thursday.

Tonight's German result is a euro-negative risk that would push this into exactly the franc strength the SNB has said it will resist, and Thursday's 07:30Z assessment plus the 08:00Z press conference is where that resistance gets restated or not. The crude leg is the swing factor - Rapidan's end-September constraint pays Canada, and a Hormuz de-escalation headline pays neither.

symbols.why: Both at 0, and the case for eventually favouring the kiwi is the canonical path rather than anything current: TE projects New Zealand trending to 4.00% in 2027 with a 3.0% forecast already attached to December 9, against Switzerland flat at 0.00%. Nothing inside the horizon supports it - New Zealand's October 28 meeting is a hold on TE's own forecast.

New Zealand's deteriorating labour market is the other side. LOW conviction.

symbols.why: Both at 0 with flat-to-lower canonical paths - TE has Canada at 2.25% then 2.00% and Switzerland at 0.00% - so this trades the commodity-versus-haven axis rather than any rate story. Right now both sides of that axis are quiet: crude fell three sessions to 100.300 while the franc's haven bid is absent, with USD/CHF +3.11% on the month.

Thursday stacks the SNB at 07:30Z against Canadian retail sales at 12:30Z. Trade the levels, small.

catalysts.event: Federal Reserve rate decision, FOMC statement and Summary of Economic Projections - Federal Reserve
catalysts.note: RELEASED. The Fed raised the target range to 3.75%-4.00%, actual 4% against a 4% consensus, TE-verified, the first hike since 2023. The rate was priced and carried no information; the projections were the event. TE's calendar carries Interest Rate Projection 1st Yr at 4.1% against 3.6% previously and 2nd Yr at 3.9% against 3.4%, with sixteen of eighteen participants projecting at least one further increase, and supporting forecasts of real GDP 2.3%, unemployment 4.1% and core PCE 3.4%. This remains the anchor for USD at +3. Note the sourcing correction made today: TE attaches no forecast to the October 28 meeting, but its model path projects 4.25% in 2027, so the canonical source carries a further hike without dating it.

catalysts.event: Bank of England rate decision, Monetary Policy Summary and MPC vote split - Bank of England
catalysts.note: RELEASED. Bank Rate held at 3.75% as forecast, but the vote was the event and TE still carries both rows explicitly: BoE MPC Vote Hike 3/9 and BoE MPC Vote Cut 0/9. Three members voted for an immediate move to 4% and not one voted to cut. Read alongside Ofgem's confirmed October energy cap rise, that is the basis of the sterling upgrade to +1, and TE's model projection of 4.00% in 2027 now carries the November move rather than merely permitting it. TE's calendar also lists December 17 with a Vote Unchanged row and a Vote Hike row scheduled, and no Vote Cut row.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan policy rate and Monetary Policy Statement - Bank of Japan
catalysts.note: RELEASED. The BoJ raised the policy rate to 1.25% from 1.00%, actual matching both the 1.25% consensus and TE's house forecast, taking borrowing costs to their highest since April 1995 on a 7-2 vote with Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato dissenting AGAINST. The gap from the previous hike was three months, the shortest since 1990. The decisive follow-through is that TE's October 30 row carries no forecast with Previous at 1.25%, while TE's model projects Japan trending around 1.00 percent in 2027 - below the current policy rate - against a Fed projected at 4.25%.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan press conference with Governor Ueda - Bank of Japan
catalysts.note: RELEASED. Ueda signalled readiness to keep raising rates and to adjust the degree of accommodation as conditions evolve, but gave no explicit guidance on the pace. Against two dissents AGAINST the hike, the market read the package as a cap rather than a signal: the yen extended losses through the conference, traded past 157 to two-week lows and closed at 156.874, +2.12% on the week and lower for an eighth consecutive session. This is the event that took JPY to -1, and it is worth recording that this page moved only after the conference happened rather than in anticipation of it.

catalysts.event: German state elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania
catalysts.note: TODAY, and the biggest unpriced risk on this page. These are the two state elections following the September 6 Saxony-Anhalt vote where the AfD came close to an outright majority. Reporting into the weekend has Merz's CDU expected to lose ground in both, with heavy losses across the pair leaving the Chancellor under immediate pressure to step aside well before the 2029 federal election. Markets closed Friday afternoon, hours before polls, so the result reaches the euro and the DAX cold at Monday's open. Not a ForexFactory calendar item, so no release time is attached here. EUR is held at 0 because the event has not resolved; GER40 goes RANGE on gap risk.

catalysts.event: Japan bank holiday - Tokyo closed (also Sep 22)
catalysts.note: Japan is shut Monday and Tuesday for back-to-back bank holidays, removing the domestic bid from the yen complex for two sessions. This matters more than a holiday usually would: intervention risk is already elevated after the Ministry of Finance bought yen twelve days ago, and a thinned tape is where intervention bites hardest and where a gap is most likely. It is a reason to size the yen crosses down rather than to stand aside.

catalysts.event: ECB President Lagarde speaks - European Central Bank (also Sep 22, 11:00Z)
catalysts.note: Lagarde speaks at 15:00Z Monday and again at 11:00Z Tuesday, which puts her in front of a microphone twice in the immediate aftermath of the German state elections. The monetary question is whether the Council treats the August HICP revision - headline down to 3.2%, services 3.0% from 3.3%, core 2.4% - as disinflation confirmed or as noise, with energy at +14.3% y/y holding the headline up. Nagel also speaks Tuesday at 08:30Z and 19:30Z, and the German Bundesbank monthly report lands Monday 10:00Z.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada Governor Macklem speaks - Bank of Canada
catalysts.note: The first read on the Bank since the September 2 hold, and the question is whether a -0.1% m/m August CPI print plus employment at -41,700 has moved the Governor toward acknowledging the labour market rather than the energy shock. TE carries no forecast at the October 28 decision and projects 2.25% into 2027 before 2.00% in 2028, so a hawkish surprise here would be a genuine repricing against a currency with no rate support. Goolsbee also speaks Monday at 10:30Z on the US side.

catalysts.event: RBA Governor Bullock speaks - Reserve Bank of Australia
catalysts.note: The single most direct test of the 80-87% pricing for a September 29 hike, coming three days after the House Economics Committee testimony where Bullock framed the open question as whether tightening delivered so far is SUFFICIENT and Hauser said rates are only now near a sensible level of long-term real rates. TE carries 4.35% unchanged at the meeting and then projects easing to 4.10% in 2027, so this is where the canonical-versus-market split either narrows or widens. Anything that softens the sufficiency framing takes the pricing apart a week before the board sits.

catalysts.event: Flash manufacturing and services PMIs - euro area, Germany, France, United Kingdom and United States
catalysts.note: The week's main data cluster. German flash services is forecast at 49.9 from 48.5 and manufacturing 54.0 from 54.1; French services 48.4 unchanged and manufacturing 50.9 from 51.5; euro-area services 51.4 from 51.7. UK services is forecast at 52.0 from 52.8 and manufacturing 51.4, which matters for a committee whose growth leg has been the least-damaged part of its case. US flash services 56.0 from 56.8 and manufacturing 53.4 from 53.2. Australian flash PMIs land Tuesday 23:00Z and Japan's Thursday 00:30Z.

catalysts.event: Australia employment change and unemployment rate (August) - Australian Bureau of Statistics
catalysts.note: The specific invalidation test for AUD at +2, three business days before the RBA board meets. Consensus is +20.9K after July's -15,827, with the unemployment rate forecast unchanged at 4.5% - note the consensus is higher than the roughly +15K this page carried on Friday, so the bar for a soft print is correspondingly higher. July's internals were the warning: full-time +16,333 against part-time -32,160 with participation slipping to 66.9%. A second consecutive contraction against a raised consensus takes the 80-87% hike pricing apart and AUD to +1.

catalysts.event: SNB monetary policy assessment and policy rate - Swiss National Bank
catalysts.note: The only scheduled central-bank decision this board is directly exposed to. TE, the ForexFactory consensus and the economist polls all carry 0.00% against a 0.00% previous, so the rate is not the event: the conditional inflation forecast is, which in June projected annual averages of 0.6% for 2026 and 2027 and 0.7% for 2028, and so is the intervention language, where June signalled a GREATER readiness to counter rapid and excessive franc appreciation. Swiss data has run hot for a zero rate - GDP 2.3% y/y, manufacturing PMI 57.1, CPI 0.8% from 0.4% - which argues for a less dovish tone than the rate implies.

catalysts.event: SNB press conference with Chairman Schlegel - Swiss National Bank
catalysts.note: Half an hour after the assessment, and the part that actually carries the risk to every franc position on this page. The question is whether an SNB under Schlegel manages the franc differently from one under Jordan, and the observable tell is the weekly sight-deposit series rather than the rhetoric. A raised conditional inflation path plus softened intervention language takes CHF to +1 and hurts USD/CHF LONG, GBP/CHF and AUD/CHF immediately; an explicit intervention threat takes CHF to -1.

catalysts.event: Bank of England MPC members Dhingra, Breeden and Lombardelli speak - Bank of England
catalysts.note: Three separate reads on the committee in five hours - Dhingra 09:30Z, Breeden 13:30Z, Lombardelli 14:00Z - a week after a hold with three members voting for 4% and none to cut. The specific thing to listen for is whether they treat Ofgem's confirmed October cap rise as a reason to tighten or as an imported shock to look through, given the same announcement zeroes VAT on domestic electricity and mechanically flatters the October CPI they will see on November 5.

catalysts.event: Canada retail sales and core retail sales (July) - Statistics Canada, and US unemployment claims
catalysts.note: Canadian retail sales are forecast at -0.8% m/m with the core measure -0.5%, after +0.6% and +0.5%. A second soft consumer print against employment at -41,700, participation at 65.0% and services PMI at 46.8 would confirm that Canada's weakness is domestic rather than energy-driven, which is the case for USD/CAD LONG independent of crude. US initial claims are forecast at 201K after 196K, with the four-week average at 203K - this page's written downgrade trigger for USD is a break back above 207K.

catalysts.event: Bank of England Governor Bailey speaks - Bank of England
catalysts.note: The most consequential sterling event of the week and the direct test of the GBP upgrade to +1. Bailey has to reconcile a confirmed administered energy increase - Ofgem's October 1 cap rise of 4% with the gas component +8% - against a labour market that has visibly cracked, with the claimant count +27.8K against an 8.3K forecast, payrolled employees -26.1K and wage growth decelerating to 3.9%. If he frames the cap rise as an imported shock to look through, the November 5 pricing this page is trading deflates and GBP goes back to 0; if he treats it as a reason three members were already right, EUR/GBP short pays.

catalysts.event: Revised University of Michigan consumer sentiment and inflation expectations (September) - University of Michigan
catalysts.note: Sentiment is forecast at 47.5 against a 47.8 preliminary, with inflation expectations previously 4.6%. This is the softest part of the dollar's case - TE has consumer confidence at 47.8, down from 51.7 - and it sits awkwardly beside retail sales at +1.2% m/m with the control group +1.4%. The inflation-expectations line is the one that matters for the Fed's projected path, because 4.6% is what makes the 3.4% core PCE projection defensible against core CPI already at 2.4%.

catalysts.event: RBA cash rate decision - Reserve Bank of Australia
catalysts.note: Nine days out and the largest scheduled divergence on the board. Market pricing is 80-87% for a 25bp move to 4.60%, with NAB, Deutsche Bank, UBS and Morgan Stanley forecasting it, ANZ and CBA carrying November, and Westpac seeing none this year. TE carries 4.35% UNCHANGED as its forecast and then projects easing to 4.10% in 2027. Meeting Minutes follow on October 13. Not this week's red folder, but it is what Tuesday's Bullock speech and Thursday's labour force survey are both priced against.

catalysts.event: BoJ Summary of Opinions and SNB Quarterly Bulletin
catalysts.note: The Summary of Opinions is the next scheduled input that can change the yen read, and the specific thing it can reveal is whether a majority pushed for October rather than accepting the pause TE's blank October 30 forecast implies - that would take JPY back to 0. The SNB's Quarterly Bulletin lands the same day at 13:00Z, six days after the assessment, and is where the conditional inflation path gets set out in full rather than summarised.

catalysts.event: ECB Monetary Policy Meeting Accounts - European Central Bank
catalysts.note: The live euro item and the next thing that can move EUR off 0 on monetary rather than political grounds. The accounts will show how the Governing Council discussed the risks on September 10, eight days before services inflation was revised down to 3.0% from 3.3% and core to 2.4%. If the Council is shown treating those series as noise while worrying about energy pass-through, EUR goes to +1 and the EUR/GBP short is the position that suffers. TE lists the September 30 non-monetary-policy meeting and the October 1 General Council before it.

catalysts.event: Strait of Hormuz transit counts, Iranian maritime enforcement and the Saudi East-West pipeline repair
catalysts.note: The undated risk that sits across CAD, USOIL, XAU, XAG and CHF simultaneously. Twelve vessels transited on September 16 against six the prior day, eleven of the twelve running dark with AIS off, against a pre-crisis baseline of 88 to 130 a day. Iran has enforced new transit rules since its 60-day ceasefire lapsed, with a fatal attack on the bulk carrier Minoan Dignity and the seizure of the tanker Amara. Rapidan reads the damaged East-West pipeline as constraining Saudi production and exports through at least end-September, with risk skewed to a larger disruption. Araghchi has claimed in Beijing that Iran agreed a plan with Oman to reopen the strait, which no Omani official has confirmed - that headline is the one that takes crude under 95.

catalysts.event: US August core PCE price index - Bureau of Economic Analysis
catalysts.note: Still the real test of the dollar's +3 and the cleanest written invalidation on this page. TE has core PCE annual at 3.3% and the Fed's own September projection at 3.4%, against core CPI that has already decelerated to 2.4% from 2.5%. Those two cannot both be right for long. Core PCE confirming the CPI deceleration undercuts the projection leg that the whole hawkish case rests on, and takes USD off +3 regardless of what October pricing does in the meantime.

geopolitics: The transmission chain this week is unchanged in structure and better documented in both directions, which is why the oil-linked positions stay two-sided rather than resolving. On the crude leg the price has been falling while the risk has not: WTI fell a third consecutive session to 100.300, -1.58%, finishing the week essentially flat at +0.25%, with Brent 103.870. The market has been weighting Saudi Arabia's workarounds above the fighting - crude loading through Oman, ship-to-ship transfers near Sohar well above August levels, and guidance that roughly half the damaged East-West pipeline capacity returns within days. The new information cuts the other way and it should be on the page: Rapidan Energy's read is that the pipeline outage constrains Saudi crude production and exports through at least the end of September, with risk skewed toward a larger disruption if the outage extends past September or if Iran, the Houthis or other proxy groups escalate attacks. That is a firmer supply constraint than Friday's framing, and prices have gained more than 5% since the drone attack from Iraq that caused it. The physical chokepoint has not reopened. Twelve vessels transited Hormuz on September 16, twice the six of the day before, but against a pre-crisis baseline of 88 to 130 a day that is still a near-closure, and eleven of the twelve ran dark with AIS switched off - a jump in dark transits that is itself the risk signal, because it means the traffic that moves is moving unobserved. Iran has been enforcing new maritime transit regulations since its 60-day ceasefire lapsed, and the enforcement has been kinetic: a fatal attack on the bulk carrier Minoan Dignity and the seizure of the tanker Amara. The diplomatic channel is running the other way at the same time, which is the instability rather than a resolution - Foreign Minister Araghchi said in Beijing that Iran has agreed a plan with Oman to reopen the strait, a claim no Omani official has confirmed. So crude is cheaper on logistics while the underlying risk is unchanged or worse, and the headline risk is genuinely two-way: a confirmed Omani reopening takes WTI under 95, a failed pipeline repair or a Hormuz escalation takes it through 110. That is why USOIL is RANGE with upward asymmetry rather than SHORT, and why CAD is held at 0 rather than cut even with spot down three sessions. On the gas leg the premium is still rising and this is where the FX consequence is cleanest and most durable. EU gas is 79.52 with the month +25.46%, German gas 80.54 with the month +25.91%, and UK gas 198.16 with the month +26.71%. Gas does not reroute on shuttle tankers the way crude does, so the European energy bill keeps rising while the oil price falls. The FX read follows from how the two European central banks have committed to treat that, and it is now visible in TE's own projections rather than only in the rhetoric: Britain is projected to trend around 4.00 percent in 2027 against today's 3.75%, with Ofgem's October 1 cap rise of 4% confirmed and the gas component up 8%, blamed explicitly on the Middle East conflict, and three of nine MPC members already voting for 4%. The euro area is projected at 2.65 percent in 2027 before cutting to 2.15 percent in 2028, with final August HICP revised down to 3.2%, services at 3.0% and core 2.4%, so what holds its headline up is energy at +14.3% y/y - an import bill, which is what the ECB looks through. Same shock, opposite reaction functions, and that is the EUR/GBP short. The remaining transmission lines are shorter. The falling crude premium pulls inflation expectations and real yields down, which is what the metals have been taking: gold 4383.45 and +0.76% on the week, silver 66.236 and +3.07% and the board's best performer, with the Silver Institute now putting 2026's deficit at 46.3 million ounces, a sixth consecutive shortfall wider than last year's. The franc's haven bid is absent for the same reason, with USD/CHF +3.11% on the month - a franc weakening through a shooting war, which is exactly what an intervention-ready SNB is engineered to produce, and Thursday's assessment is where that gets restated or not. German equities take the gas leg directly, with GER40 down 1.60% on Friday to 25,304 led by autos, Volkswagen -5.97%, Porsche -5.19% and Mercedes -4.76%. And the one commodity position here that is not war-driven is copper, whose squeeze is tariff-arbitrage driven - LME stocks drained to roughly 90,000 tonnes and cash more than 550 dollars over three-month futures - which means a trade resolution could unwind it rather than intensify it, and at 6.6150 it trades far above the 10,000-11,000 dollar range Goldman carries for 2026.
